c:add_parameter.why: RE-VERDICTED 2026-08-26 (phase-379 W5), was `rename`. rclc declares a parameter with `rclc_add_parameter(server, name, TYPE)` and gives it a value in a second `rclc_parameter_set_*` call. Ours is `nros_parameter_declare_<type>(server, name, DEFAULT)` -- one call, which is rclcpp's and rclrs's shape, so the FOLD is deliberate. The two are not one call under two names: rclc's third argument is a TYPE (`rclc_parameter_type_t`, confirmed in the recorded rclc surface), ours is a VALUE. So no target name exists for this row to carry -- which is exactly why it sat blocked, and a row that endorses our shape and can name no destination is a DECLINE, not a rename. What a user loses: the two-step idiom; a ported rclc node rewrites `rclc_add_parameter(s, "x", RCLC_PARAMETER_INT)` + `rclc_parameter_set_int(s, "x", 5)` as one `nros_parameter_declare_integer(s, "x", 5)`. The reader's other complaint -- that nothing here is spelled `add` -- is really the `param` vs `parameter` PREFIX question, and that is a DIFFERENT row: `c:parameter_server_t` owns it. Ours half: the `c:parameter_declare_*` family.

rename.resolution: re-verdicted `declined` -- the declare/set fold means rclc's call and ours take different arguments, so no rename target exists; the prefix question is c:parameter_server_t's, not this row's

c:add_parameter_constraint_double.why: OUR LANGUAGES DISAGREE: our Rust has the whole descriptor surface -- `ParameterDescriptor::with_description` / `with_read_only` / `with_integer_range` / `with_float_range` / `with_dynamic_typing`, plus `validate_range` enforced on every set -- and our C has NO descriptor surface whatever. The `~/describe_parameters` server a C user registers with `nros_executor_register_parameter_services` therefore answers with empty descriptors for everything that C declared. Phase 379 W3. rclc attaches a `[from, to, step]` range to a double parameter and REJECTS sets outside it; our C accepts anything the type allows.

The `~/describe_parameters` server a C user registers with `nros_executor_register_parameter_services` therefore answers with empty descriptors for everything that C declared. Phase 379 W3. rclc attaches a description and an additional-constraints string to a declared parameter; nothing in `nros/parameter.h` takes either.

c:bool_array_t.why: a parsed `bool[]` sequence, heap-allocated by the YAML parser. `rcl_yaml_param_parser` exists to parse a `--params-file` off a FILESYSTEM at node start and hand rcl a tree of overrides. A device image has no filesystem and no YAML parser; parameter defaults are baked into the image at build time (RFC-0045) and changed afterwards over `~/set_parameters`. What a user loses is `--params-file` and everything that reads one.

c:delete_parameter.why: OUR LANGUAGES DISAGREE: rclc can undeclare a parameter at runtime, and so can our Rust (`ParameterServer::remove`, and `ParameterServer::unset` to clear the value while keeping the declaration). C has neither, and C++ has neither -- `nros/parameter.h` and `nros/parameter.hpp` offer declare/get/set/has/count/fini and no way to take a parameter back. Nothing about static storage forbids it; the slot is a fixed array entry that `ParameterServer::remove` already clears one language over. Phase 379 W3.

c:executor_add_parameter_server.why: rclc attaches a CALLER-OWNED `rclc_parameter_server_t` to the executor. Ours is `nros_executor_register_parameter_services(executor)`, which takes no server because the executor owns the only one there is -- static entity storage, no allocator to make a second. Ledgered as an extension in the service stage. Note which of our TWO C parameter stores this is. `nros_parameter_server_t` (`nros/parameter.h`) is a standalone store over caller-supplied storage and is purely node-local -- `parameter.rs` calls it "the legacy `nros_parameter_server_t` API" in its own comment. The store the six `rcl_interfaces/srv/*` servers read is a DIFFERENT object, the `nros_params::ParameterServer` the executor owns, reached only through `nros_executor_*_param_*`. Nothing joins them. What a user additionally loses is rclc's on-modification callback, which this call is where you pass: see `c:executor_add_parameter_server_with_context`.

c:executor_add_parameter_server_with_con.why: the `void* context` form -- and the row that matters, because BOTH rclc forms take the on-modification callback and ours takes none. So a `ros2 param set` reaching the executor-owned store notifies nobody: the C callback that does exist, `nros_parameter_server_set_callback`, is on the legacy standalone `nros_parameter_server_t`, which is not the object the services write to. Note which of our TWO C parameter stores this is. `nros_parameter_server_t` (`nros/parameter.h`) is a standalone store over caller-supplied storage and is purely node-local -- `parameter.rs` calls it "the legacy `nros_parameter_server_t` API" in its own comment. The store the six `rcl_interfaces/srv/*` servers read is a DIFFERENT object, the `nros_params::ParameterServer` the executor owns, reached only through `nros_executor_*_param_*`. Nothing joins them. NOTE FOR RFC-0036: line 91 says "No parameter callbacks; parameters are read/write only", and that is now wrong in both directions -- C ships an accept/reject set-callback on one store, and has none on the store `ros2 param` talks to. Phase 379 W3.

c:executor_allow_undeclared_parameters.why: the C spelling of `rust:Executor::allow_undeclared_parameters`, and it exists for the same reason the Rust one does: upstream's `allow_undeclared_parameters` is a NODE OPTION given at construction (rclcpp `NodeOptions`, rclrs `allow_undeclared`), and there is no `NodeOptions` object here to carry it -- a node is a row in the executor's fixed table, so the option is a call on the executor. The SEMANTICS are upstream's: per node, off by default (issue 1151). phase-426 W5 added it because C could not reach the policy AT ALL: `nros_executor_set_param_*` on an undeclared name was a permanent `NROS_RET_NOT_FOUND` with no opt-in, so a rule that Rust and a remote `ros2 param set` both honour was unreachable from the C API that shares the store. What a user loses: it cannot be given at node-construction time, so it must be set before `nros_executor_register_parameter_services` starts answering.

c:executor_allow_undeclared_parameters_o.why: the node-naming half of `c:executor_allow_undeclared_parameters`; see `c:executor_declare_param_*_on` for why the node is an argument here and a receiver upstream.

c:executor_declare_param_*.why: the service-backed parameter API: it operates on the `nros_params::ParameterServer` the EXECUTOR owns, which is the store `nros_executor_register_parameter_services` exposes to `ros2 param`. rclc has no equivalent spelling because rclc hands the executor a caller-owned server instead (`c:executor_add_parameter_server`); with static entity storage and no allocator there is one server and the executor holds it, so the executor is the handle. Gated on the `param-services` Cargo feature, which needs `alloc`. SCALARS ONLY -- bool/integer/double/string -- where the local `c:parameter_declare_*` family covers all ten `rcl_interfaces` types, so no C caller can publish an array parameter to `ros2 param`. This spelling means the executor's PRIMARY node; `c:executor_declare_param_*_on` names another. Phase 379 W3; phase-426 W1/W5.

c:executor_declare_param_*_on.why: phase-426 W5 -- the node-naming half of `c:executor_declare_param_*`, and the C mirror of `rust:Executor::declare_parameter_on`. The parameter STORE is one fixed table owned by the EXECUTOR, not a container per node: there is no allocator to make a second, so a node cannot own its own. Upstream keys parameters by making the node the RECEIVER (`rclcpp::Node::declare_parameter`, rclc's `rclc_parameter_server_t` bound to a node); ours are on the executor and the node is an ARGUMENT, because an image composes several nodes onto one executor (RFC-0047) and the shared table has to be told whose parameter it is. The `_on` suffix is the same disambiguation the entity builders already use (`node_mut(id)` / `_on(...)`, phase 104.C) and the same pair Rust ships, so C and Rust name one relationship one way. It is a NEW NAME rather than a widened signature deliberately: RFC-0089 permits a signature change only where the compiler forces the edit, and the existing spellings are not wrong -- they mean the primary node and will go on meaning it -- so re-signing them would cost every C caller an edit that buys nothing. What a user loses: a ported node writes `nros_executor_declare_param_integer_on(&exec, &node, name, value)` where rclcpp writes `node->declare_parameter(name, value)`. Takes the `nros_node_t` rather than its slot index, so a node that is uninitialised or bound to another executor is refused instead of silently meaning slot 0.

c:executor_get_param_*_on.why: the read half of the per-node family; see `c:executor_declare_param_*_on`.

c:executor_has_param_on.why: the existence predicate of the per-node family; see `c:executor_declare_param_*_on`. Upstream's correspondent is `rclcpp::Node::has_parameter`, whose receiver IS the node. A node this executor does not own answers `false`, never the primary node's answer -- defaulting the node is how a sibling's parameter reads as this one's.

c:executor_set_param_*_on.why: the write half of the per-node family; see `c:executor_declare_param_*_on`. Routes through `Executor::set_parameter_on`, hence `ParameterServer::apply`, so a C set gets exactly the read-only / type / range / undeclared rules a remote `ros2 param set` gets (phase-426 W2).

c:param_array_t.why: the deprecated `nros_param_*` spelling of `c:parameter_array_t`. DEPRECATED ALIAS, phase-379 W5 (2026-08-27). The live spelling is `nros_parameter_array_t`; this one survived one release as a plain `typedef` in `nros/parameter.h`; phase-417 W-B5 (stage 6 step B, commit 4dc5caee9, 2026-09-05) retired all four typedef aliases with the forwarders, so the old type name is an error now. It compiles SILENTLY -- C has no portable way to attach a deprecation attribute to a typedef (MSVC rejects `__declspec(deprecated)` there and `[[deprecated]]` on one is C23), so unlike the function forwarders this alias is a grace period rather than a warning, and this row is where the deprecation is actually recorded. It aliases the TYPE NAME only: `struct nros_param_array_t` no longer names anything, because the tag moved with the type. Removal is no longer the follow-up; it happened in W-B5. Substantive verdict moved to `c:parameter_array_t`.

rename.residue: NONE since phase-417 W-B5 (stage 6 step B, commit 4dc5caee9, 2026-09-05), which retired the four typedef aliases beside the forwarders. Removal is no longer the follow-up; it happened in W-B5. Substantive verdict moved to `c:parameter_declare_*`.

rust:ParameterStorage.why: backing storage for a `ParameterServer`, which rclrs has no counterpart to because rclrs allocates -- its parameters live behind the `Arc<Node>`'s mutex and grow on demand. Constraint: no allocator, so the slots must be memory the CALLER placed (a `static`, a struct field, or the executor backing once phase-382 W3' carves it) and lent for the server's life. `N` defaults to `MAX_PARAMETERS`, the Kconfig-derived constant, and is not a cap. This row covers every `ParameterStorage::*` member; `init_in_place` is worth naming because the type is enormous and scales with `N` (285,184 bytes at 32 slots, 2,281,472 at 256 -- `ParameterValue` is sized by its `StringArray` variant), so `Box::new(ParameterStorage::new())` builds the whole value on the stack first and overruns an RTOS thread stack (issue 0756). It moved here from `ParameterServer` in phase-382 W2', with the bulk it guards.

rust:ParameterTable.why: the borrowed view of a `ParameterStorage` that a `ParameterServer` holds -- `&'s mut [Option<ParameterEntry>]` behind a newtype. rclrs has no counterpart for the same reason as `rust:ParameterStorage`: it allocates, so nothing there has to name the storage separately from the store. Constraint: no allocator plus a private slot layout. The newtype exists so a consumer that must NAME the storage (`nros-node`, which will carve it out of the executor backing in phase-382 W3') can do so without `ParameterEntry` becoming public API. Its length is the server's capacity.

The row said in prose what its verdict denied: "a rename rclrs should make, not us". `rename` means OURS is the one that should change, so the row was self-contradictory, and it is the one item in this class whose misfiling had a MECHANICAL consequence -- `scripts/check-prelude-tiers.py` keys prelude membership on `extension`, so an earlier attempt to move this row into that bucket would have evicted `ParameterType` from `nros::prelude`, a name every ported parameter node needs (`packages/api/nros/src/lib.rs`). `their-rename` says the correspondent EXISTS, which is exactly the fact the prelude rule asks for, so the name stays exported and the gate now says so on purpose rather than by omission. rust:ParameterValue::*.why: typed accessors (`as_bool`, `as_string`, `as_double_array`, ...) and constructors (`from_bool`, `from_string`, ...) on the value enum. rclrs converts through `From`/`TryFrom` impls that hand back owned `String`/`Vec`; ours cannot, because the value is stored in a `heapless::String<MAX_STRING_VALUE_LEN>` / `heapless::Vec<_, MAX_ARRAY_LEN>` inside the server's fixed slot and there is no allocator to copy it out of. So the readers return BORROWS (`Option<&str>`, `Option<&[u8]>`) and the writers are fallible on capacity (`from_string` returns `Option<Self>`). Constraint: no allocator, compile-time capacity. Same reason `rust:ParameterVariant::*` exists.

rust:ParameterValueError.why: RE-VERDICTED 2026-08-26 (phase-379 W5), was `rename`, and the old reason was wrong on two counts. rclrs's set-time failure enum is exactly `OutOfRange`, `TypeMismatch`, `ReadOnly` (recorded surface: rclrs 0.7.0, `rclrs/src/parameter.rs`). It is one of rclrs's TWO parameter error enums -- the other is `DeclarationError` (`AlreadyDeclared`, `NoValueAvailable`, `OverrideValueTypeMismatch`, `PriorValueTypeMismatch`, `InitialValueOutOfRange`, `InvalidRange`). Ours is ONE `ParameterError` (`packages/core/nros-params/src/typed.rs:18`) whose seven variants span both: those three, plus `InvalidRange` -- which is rclrs's DECLARATION error, and ours is raised by `ParameterBuilder::integer_range`/`float_range` -- plus `NotFound`, plus `StorageFull` and `StringConversion`, the two failures a fixed-capacity `heapless` store has and an allocating one does not. So (a) it is NOT 'the same concept under a different name': our declare path already returns it (`ParameterBuilder::mandatory`/`optional`/`read_only` -> `Result<_, ParameterError>`), and a type called `ParameterValueError` would report a full store and a malformed range as 'value' errors. And (b) it is not 'no platform reason': two of the four extra variants are the capacity constraint made visible, the same one `rust:ParameterValue::*` and `rust:ParameterVariant::*` record. Taking rclrs's narrow name would also fight `rust:DeclarationError`, the open gap for the other half of rclrs's split. What a user loses: that split -- a type-level distinction between a declare-time and a set-time failure -- which is recorded as the `rust:DeclarationError` gap, not here. Ours half: `rust:ParameterError`.

rename.resolution: re-verdicted `declined` -- ours is not a renamed ParameterValueError but a union of rclrs's ParameterValueError and DeclarationError plus two heapless-capacity variants; the missing split is the rust:DeclarationError gap

rust:ParameterVariant::*.why: `to_parameter_value` / `from_parameter_value` / `try_to_parameter_value` -- the conversion trait between a Rust type and a stored `ParameterValue`. rclrs's `ParameterVariant` declares only `kind()` and does its conversions through `From`. The third method is the constraint made visible: `to_parameter_value` cannot report that a `String` exceeded `MAX_STRING_VALUE_LEN` or a `Vec` exceeded `MAX_ARRAY_LEN`, and the hosted impls used to `unwrap_or_default()` -- turning an over-long string into `NotSet` (a TYPE change) and an oversized vec into an EMPTY array, both indistinguishable from a caller who meant it (issue 0323). Fixed capacity forces a fallible conversion; an allocator would not. See `rust:ParameterValue::*`.

rust:default_initial_value_discriminator.why: the default choice function over `rust:AvailableValues`. rclrs's parameter OVERRIDE machinery: a value supplied outside the code (`--ros-args -p`, a params file, a prior declaration) that the declaration then has to reconcile with. cpp:declared_param_node.why: phase-446 W6. The declaring node for a namespace + name in the generated `declared_params` table (`nros/declared_params.hpp`), or `nullptr` when the node's launch contract has no `params:`. rclcpp has no counterpart: its parameters are declared nowhere outside the code, so there is nothing to check a declaration against. Ours are declared in the launch contract because the parameter store is a fixed table sized from that contract at build time (no allocator to grow it, phase-446 W4), and `ComponentNode::declare_parameter` uses this lookup to refuse, at boot, a declaration the contract does not make. `constexpr`, so `declared_params.cpp` asserts its answers against a rendered fixture.
